newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt tells Israel peace must be balanced.
newsitem.headline: Egypt tells Israel peace must be balanced.

text.p: Egypt told Israel on Thursday it must negotiate balanced agreements with its neighbours, not try to impose peace on its own terms.

"Peace, in order to last...has to be balanced between the Israelis and the Palestinians, not to be imposed but to be agreed upon," Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said after he and President Hosni Mubarak met Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy.

"Balance, agreement and fairness were the points stressed by the president...Any progress that Arab public opinion would accept, and in fact international public opinion would accept, is a fair peace between the Palestinians and Israelis (and that) would certainly help the other tracks too," he told reporters.
Talks between the Jewish state and Syria and Lebanon have been stalled for years over Israeli withdrawal from lands it occupied in a 1967 war.
Progress on peace talks between Israel and the Palestinians has been slow since the May election of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who refuses to trade Arab land for peace.

Negotiations are currently snagged on a long-delayed Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron that was stipulated in a peace agreement that Netanayahu is now trying to alter for security reasons.

The Palestinians say the deal should be implemented as signed and Mubarak, whose country became in 1979 the first Arab state to make peace with Israel, has said he would not meet Netanyahu unless there was total agreement on the status of Hebron.

Levy, in Cairo to ease recent strains in the Jewish state's ties with Egypt, described his meeting with Mubarak as excellent and said Israel and Egypt would work together to advance the peace process.

"The meeting was excellent...relations between Egypt and Israel are very important and peace between the two states can be a model for the rest of the parties and we have moved together to promote the peace process," Levy said.

"It is clear that we must solve together matters between us and the Palestinians but peace comes from all parties and it's natural that on the way to implementation there will be obstacles and problems," he added.
Arabs have attacked what they see as Netanyahu's "anti-peace" policies, which include lifting a ban on building Jewish settlements on occupied lands.

Official Egypt has also joined in the criticism and its government-run press has run pages of vitrolic comments against the Israeli prime minister. Some dailies have even said that he and his government resemble a criminal gang.

Levy has rebuked Egypt's ambassador to Israel for the disparaging press and Israel's Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon had said no one from his ministry would attend next week's regional economic summit in Cairo because Egypt's leaders and papers had been attacking the Israeli government.
